newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Rosenthal details measures to forge recovery.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rosenthal details measures to forge recovery.

text.p: Sweeping changes lie in store for German porcelain maker Rosenthal, which on Friday announced terms of a rights issue which will deepen its alliance with Ireland's Waterford Wedgwood.

Rosenthal said it had narrowed its loss in 1996 to 4.6 million marks ($2.7 million) from 15.9 million marks, despite continued sluggishness in German consumer demand, while turnover was down three percent at 320.4 million marks from 330.4 million marks.
The company also announced a series of restructuring measures aimed at turning around its fortunes.

Key to the success of the restructuring is a capital increase which Rosenthal's supervisory board approved on Friday. Shareholders will be offered 300,000 shares at 120 marks each from April 14 through April 28.

The issue will be guaranteed by Irish porcelain and crystal group Waterford Wedgwood, which currently holds a 9.1 percent stake in Rosenthal, and is seeking to widen its alliance with the German firm.

Waterford Wedgwood's stake in Rosenthal will increase to at least 12.5 percent after the capital increase and Waterford Wedgwood chief Richard Barnes said that the group had secured the preferred rights in question with two options.
Another major shareholder, the Bavarian bank Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank AG (Hypo-Bank), which holds a 9.9 percent stake, also said it would take part in the rights issue.
Rosenthal also said that it had reserved some 40 million marks to pay for further restructuring measures.

"Because of changes in the company and as a result of the structural crisis at the group which has yet to be resolved, we think it necessary to introduce further restructuring measures which will hit earnings in 1996," the group said.
The restructuring programme will involve cutting the payroll by around 600 employees, management board chairman Otmar Kuesel told a news conference on Friday.
In 1996 Rosenthal had around 2,200 employees, of which 2,050 are in Germany. This is way down on the group's payroll of 4,000 in the early 1990s.
Kuesel said that the group would seek to focus its production, which could involve closing factories or shifting production to other factories within the group.
There was no question of shifting production abroad, Kuesel said, but the group was expecting to sell more produce in foreign markets.

The porcelain industry had been badly hit by sluggish consumer demand in Germany, but Rosenthal was doing better than some its rivals. Overall industry sales had fallen six percent in 1996, but sales at Rosenthal had only fallen by three percent, Kuesel said.
Achieving breakeven in 1997 would be difficult, Kuesel said, and would not give a forecast when Rosenthal would resume paying dividends.
Shares in Rosenthal ended bourse trade in Frankfurt on Friday up two marks at 130 marks.
